content.title: About
content.content: Bell peppers (Capsicum annuum) are crisp, juicy, hollow fruits native to Central and South America. They come in green, red, yellow, orange, and sometimes purple, and have a mild, sweet to slightly bitter flavor. Unlike chili peppers, they contain no capsaicin and are not spicy. They are eaten raw, cooked, stuffed, or used in sauces and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically, bell peppers are fruits, classified as a type of berry.
Color usually reflects ripeness: green peppers are unripe, while red peppers are fully ripe and typically sweeter.
Bell peppers lack capsaicin because of a gene that prevents its production, so they taste mild.
Red bell peppers generally contain more vitamin C and carotenoids than green ones.
Bell peppers are also called sweet peppers in many countries.

items.title: Very rich in vitamin C
items.content: Bell peppers, especially red ones, are an excellent source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: Red, orange, and yellow peppers contain carotenoids that the body can partly convert into vitamin A.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6 and folate
items.content: These vitamins support normal metabolism and cell function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids help protect cells against oxidative damage.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Bell peppers are low in calories and high in water, making them a refreshing snack.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people, especially those with pollen allergies, may experience itching or tingling in the mouth after eating raw peppers.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Raw bell peppers may cause bloating or gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Nightshade sensitivity
items.content: Bell peppers belong to the nightshade family, and some people report sensitivity to these vegetables.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Conventionally grown peppers may carry residues, so wash them thoroughly before eating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bell peppers can be eaten raw in salads, as snacks with dips, or sliced into sandwiches. They can be roasted, grilled, sautéed, stuffed with rice or meat, or added to soups, stews, and sauces. Roasting brings out their natural sweetness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole, unwashed bell peppers in the refrigerator crisper drawer, where they usually keep for one to two weeks. Cut peppers should be kept in an airtight container and used within a few days. Peppers can also be sliced and frozen for cooking.

cereal-or-granola-bar-peanuts-oats-sugar.title: Cereal or Granola Bar with Peanuts, Oats, Sugar and Wheat Germ

content.title: About
content.content: This cereal bar combines whole oat flakes, roasted peanuts, a touch of sugar, and nutrient‑dense wheat germ. It offers a convenient snack rich in complex carbohydrates, plant protein, and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are among the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 10,000 years.
Peanuts are botanically legumes, not true nuts.
Wheat germ contains higher levels of B‑vitamins and minerals than the endosperm.
Sugar in bars acts as a sweetener and a binder that holds the ingredients together.
Granola, the basis of many bars, became popular with mountaineers in the early 20th century as a lightweight, energy‑dense food.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oats and wheat germ provide soluble and insoluble fiber that supports digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Peanuts and oats supply a complete set of essential amino acids useful for muscle repair and recovery.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Peanuts are rich in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that promote heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Wheat germ is a good source of vitamin E, magnesium, zinc, and iron, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The blend of complex carbs and a modest amount of sugar provides a quick and sustained energy release.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are a strong allergen; individuals with peanut allergy should avoid this product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even a small amount of sugar can be an issue for those monitoring glycemic load.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bars are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: Wheat germ and oats may contain gluten; the product is not suitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar is handy for on‑the‑go snacking, at work, or in the gym. It can be eaten plain, crumbled into yogurt or kefir, or chopped and used as a topping for ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them refrigerated to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat flakes cereal consists of thin, dry sheets made from whole grain wheat that have been steamed, toasted, and rolled. They have a light crunchy texture, a mild nutty flavor, and are commonly used as a breakfast base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flakes made from whole wheat retain most of the grain’s fiber and vitamins.
The production process includes heat treatment, which improves digestibility.
Wheat is one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown by humans for over 10,000 years.
Commercial flakes are often fortified with B‑vitamins, iron, and folic acid.
In many countries they are served with milk, yogurt, fruit, or used in baking.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide a steady release of energy and maintain stable glucose levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, and niacin are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Flakes provide iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, essential for blood formation, muscle function, and bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many ready‑to‑eat breakfasts, wheat flakes contain little fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat or gluten intolerance may experience allergic reactions when consuming the flakes.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Despite the fiber content, flakes can raise blood sugar quickly, especially when eaten without protein or fat.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Some commercial versions contain sugar, flavorings, or preservatives, which can diminish their nutritional value.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wheat flakes are typically poured over milk, kefir, or a plant‑based drink and left to soften for a few minutes. They can be added to yogurt, smoothies, used in granola bars, or incorporated into baked goods such as muffins and energy bars.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the flakes in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

cookie-marshmallow-with-rice-cereal-and-.title: Cookie with Marshmallow, Rice Cereal and Chocolate Chips

content.title: About
content.content: The cookie combines soft marshmallow, crunchy rice cereal and sweet chocolate chips. It is designed for sweet‑tooth lovers who want a variety of flavors and textures in one treat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Marshmallows originated in ancient Egypt as a medicinal confection.
Rice cereal adds lightness and crunch to baked goods.
Chocolate chips are a staple in classic American chocolate chip cookies.
The marshmallow‑rice combination is popular in many Asian desserts.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from rice cereal and the sugar in marshmallow provide a quick source of energy.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Chocolate chips are rich in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: The sweet taste and chocolate aroma stimulate serotonin production, enhancing mood.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookie typically contains wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Marshmallow and chocolate chips make the product sweet, so individuals with diabetes should limit consumption.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: Crunchy cereal and sweet ingredients can lead to rapid over‑consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, crumble it into milkshakes, use it in dessert salads, or sprinkle it as a topping for ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to maintain cereal crunch and prevent chocolate melting.

content.title: About
content.content: Flavored rice mixture with cheese is a ready‑to‑cook blend of parboiled rice, seasonings and dried cheese powder. When rehydrated with hot water or milk, it becomes a creamy, aromatic side dish that can be served alone or alongside meat and vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix is popular in school cafeterias and backpacking meals because it cooks quickly.
The cheese component is usually a dry milk powder that regains flavor after hydration.
Typical spices include paprika, garlic and dried herbs, giving the dish a distinctive aroma.
Shelf life of the dry product can reach up to 12 months when stored properly.
In many countries the product is sold under different brand names, but the basic recipe remains similar.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides a fast‑acting source of energy suitable for active lifestyles.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: The cheese powder adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dry mix has a modest fat content, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Provides some protein
items.content: Cheese powder contributes a modest amount of plant‑based protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The dried cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to dairy.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The blend often contains added salt; those watching sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: May contain gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Some manufacturers process the mix on equipment that also handles gluten‑containing foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour the specified amount of hot water (or milk) over the mix, cover, and let stand for 5‑7 minutes. Optional additions include fresh vegetables, herbs, or diced ham for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place, tightly sealed. After opening, transfer to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption.
